evidence_quotes.quote: In this study, the qualitative method of participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE) was used to investigate the access of infrastructural services for female-headed household groups in the informal settlement of Vingunguti in Dar es Salaam.

The objective of this research was to investigate the problems of daily life faced by female-headed households in a people’s settlement in Dar es Salaam through participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE).

According to an informant, it had become increasingly difficult to access medical care. The respondent claimed that formal requirements for accessing medical care had increased, and “one had to have a registered address,” which is difficult to obtain in an informal setting (Figure 4).

Of the informant group representing female-headed households, only 11 were able to take photos and participate in a discussion of these photos. In addition, six of them took part in a focus group discussion.

In general, they called water scarcity a critical issue that heavily affected their livelihoods due to limited services and poor quality. All stated that there was a lack of water, at least seasonally.
One informant reported that although the area had water pipes, no water had been distributed here since 2006.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to water and sanitation infrastructure in the informal settlement of Vingunguti, Dar es Salaam, including tap water queuing, abandoned public wells, dry municipal pipes, and pit latrines.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study does not examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation access; informality is solely the descriptive setting of the study, and the paper focuses on documenting everyday infrastructural problems and evaluating participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE) as a participatory method. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure) governing water or sanitation access is analysed—the only documentation rule mentioned in the text ('one had to have a registered address') pertains strictly to accessing medical care, and connection cost is mentioned only for electricity.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical research note based on participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE), individual interviews in Swahili (n = 11), and a focus group discussion (n = 6) conducted in July–August 2009.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative household-level findings on water scarcity, queuing and conflict at taps, absence of piped municipal water distribution since 2006, seasonal water shortages and contamination, and pit latrine fullness and non-functionality.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (female-headed households in Vingunguti, Dar es Salaam), study design (qualitative PDPE interviews and focus group), general informal-settlement infrastructural context, and water/sanitation access outcomes, though no water/sanitation governance exposure is present.

study_design: Qualitative participatory study using participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE), individual interviews, and a focus group discussion
population_and_sample: Female-headed households in the Vingunguti informal settlement, Dar es Salaam (18 households selected via snowball sampling; 11 completed photo-elicitation and individual interviews, and 6 participated in a focus group discussion)
exposure: Everyday infrastructural conditions in an informal settlement (no legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation access is examined; formal registered-address requirements are reported only for medical care)
outcome: Perceived household water scarcity, queuing at taps, lack of municipal piped water distribution since 2006, seasonal water quantity and contamination variations, and full or broken pit latrines
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this qualitative photo-elicitation study empirically documents household water scarcity, dry municipal pipes, and full or broken pit latrines among female-headed households in an informal settlement in Dar es Salaam, it does not examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation access under either the plain or narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. The study focuses on describing daily infrastructural hardships and evaluating the participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE) research method, while the only formal documentation barrier mentioned ('registered address') applies exclusively to accessing medical care.
